new_statements.quote: In a verb, the stressed syllable is usually the verb itself, as opposed to any prefix or suffix. If, however, a suffix ending with {'} is separated from the verb by at least one other suffix, both the verb and the suffix ending in {'} are stressed. In addition, if the meaning of any particular suffix is to be emphasized, the stress may shift to that syllable. [...] In a noun, the stressed syllable is usually the syllable right before the first noun suffix, or the final syllable if there is no suffix. If, however, a syllable ending in {'} is present, it is usually stressed instead. If there are two syllables in a row {'} both ending in {',} both are equally stressed.
new_statements.citation: Okrand, Marc. 1992. The Klingon Dictionary: English/Klingon, Klingon/English. 2nd ed. New York: Pocket Books (ISBN 0-671-74559-X), section 1.3 'Stress', pp. 17-18.
new_statements.locator: Section 1.3 Stress, pp. 17-18 (transcript lines 527-553; page break [[p.18]] follows the section)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Klingonska Akademien proofread scanned transcription of Okrand 1992, The Klingon Dictionary, 2nd ed., Pocket Books, ISBN 0-671-74559-X; header lists the book's identity and the 2000-2020 correction log). Section "1.3. Stress" is at transcript lines 527-553, exactly as the reader states. The quoted passage is there verbatim, allowing for line-wrap joins and the marked "[...]" elision (the elided sentence is "Suffixes indicating negation or emphasis (section 4.3) are frequently stressed, as is the interrogative suffix (section 4.2.9)."); the stray "{'}" before "both ending in" is in the transcript as the reader notes. Surrounding text read: "Each Klingon word of more than one syllable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per polysyllabic word, realised by higher pitch and more force. Stress is morphologically anchored: in verbs it falls on the verb root (never on the pronominal prefix or suffixes by default); in nouns it falls on the last syllable of the noun stem (the syllable before the first noun suffix, or the final syllable of an unsuffixed noun). Overriding this, any syllable closed by the glottal stop {'} attracts stress (in verbs, a {'}-final suffix separated from the root by another suffix takes stress alongside the root; in nouns a {'}-final syllable is 'usually stressed instead'; two adjacent {'}-final syllables are both stressed). Pragmatic emphasis can shift stress to a suffix; negation/emphatic rovers and the interrogative suffix are frequently stressed. Stress is not written.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as 'secondary'; but the source allows two stressed syllables in one word: verb root plus a {'}-final suffix separated from it ('both... are stressed'), and two adjacent {'}-final syllables 'both are equally stressed'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'there are some words which seem to have variable stress patterns, with the stress sometimes heard on one syllable and sometimes on another. This phenomenon is not yet understood.' Stress may also shift to any suffix whose meaning is emphasised; negation/emphasis suffixes (sect. 4.3) and the interrogative suffix (4.2.9) are frequently stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Each Klingon word of more than one syllable normally contains one stressed (or accented) syllable'); rules given separately for verbs and nouns; no phrase-level statement. Stress is not indicated in the transcription system. Quote is from a fan scanned transcription (Klingonska Akademien, proofread 2000-2020) of the printed book, not a page image; the stray '{'}' before 'both ending in' in the last sentence is a transcription artefact.
new_statements.identity_note: Klingon is a constructed language (Marc Okrand for Paramount's Star Trek films, 1984-); Glottolog 5.1 classes it under 'Artificial Language' and lists no descriptive references. The description is of Okrand's standard variety (ta' Hol); KGT 1997 mentions regional 'accents' (Krotmag, Morska etc.) but these concern segments, not stress. Whether a conlang belongs in the catalog is a policy decision for the parent; the stress statement itself is first-hand and explicit.

sources.note: Sect. 1.3 (pp. 17-18): each polysyllabic word normally has one stressed syllable (higher pitch, more force). Verbs: stress on the verb root, not prefix/suffix; a suffix ending in glottal stop {'} separated from the root by another suffix is also stressed; emphasis (negation/emphatic rovers, interrogative -'a') can pull stress onto a suffix. Nouns: stress on the syllable right before the first noun suffix (= stem-final), or the final syllable if unsuffixed; a syllable ending in {'} is usually stressed instead; two adjacent {'}-final syllables are equally stressed. sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Klingon language', section Phonology > Stress (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Okrand 1992 (TKD) p. 17.
sources.note: Paraphrases TKD 1.3: verbs stressed on the verbal stem, plus any {'}-final suffix separated by another suffix; nouns stressed on the final stem syllable, shifting to {'}-final syllables; other words variable but mostly monosyllabic. Second-hand summary of the primary source (this is what the earlier scan read).

sources.citation: Okrand, Marc. 1997. Klingon for the Galactic Traveler. New York: Pocket Books. ISBN 0-671-00995-8.
sources.note: No stress rule restated; incidental only: younger speakers reduce doubled consonants in qettaH / bommey 'with stress remaining on the first syllable' (pp. 138-139), unstressed a may centralise to [U] (p. 139); regional 'accents' (Krotmag etc., p. 26 ff.) concern segments, not stress. Klingonska Akademien transcription.
